from.place: Proof paragraph 2, middle derived mapping-complex comparison before the inverse limit: Infinity-categorical monadicity and the augmented counit bar resolution. Supporting foundation: Free coherent monad modules and their augmented free resolution. Supporting lemma: Underlying equivalences and operadic colimits of coherent modules. Supporting step: Coherent modules as inert-preserving simplicial sections. Simplicial approximation to the left-module operad, before constructing the fixed-algebra fibration.

title: Cut and left-module prism are colour-equivalent operadic approximations
statement:
Use the operadic fibrations, category $L=N(\mathsf{LM}^{\otimes})$, pure-algebra subcategory $A$, inert arrows and sections of [def-coef-left-module-operadic-encoding], and coherent functor categories of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $D=N(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}})$, where $[n]=\{0,\ldots,n\}$. Define $\mathrm{LCut}:D\to L$ by $[n]\mapsto(\langle n+1\rangle,\{n+1\})$. For $\beta=\alpha^{\mathrm{op}}:[n]\to[m]$, with $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ monotone, its pointed map sends the indices $\alpha(j-1)<i\leq\alpha(j)$ to $j$ for $1\leq j\leq m$, sends $\alpha(m)<i\leq n+1$ to $m+1$, and sends $i\leq\alpha(0)$ to $*$. All non-basepoint fibres have their increasing order. Define $\mathrm{Cut}:D\to A$ by $[n]\mapsto(\langle n\rangle,\varnothing)$ and the same middle blocks, sending also all indices $i>\alpha(m)$ to $*$. The inert projection $\theta_n:\mathrm{LCut}([n])\to\mathrm{Cut}([n])$ discards index $n+1$ and fixes $1,\ldots,n$. These maps define the natural transformation $\gamma:D\times\Delta^1\to L$ from $\mathrm{LCut}$ to $\mathrm{Cut}$.

Both $\mathrm{Cut}:D\to A$ and $\gamma:D\times\Delta^1\to L$ are approximations in the sense of [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction]. Each induces an equivalence on its colour fibre over $\langle1\rangle$: the former fibre is the single object $[1]$ and maps to $a$; the latter fibre has exactly the two discrete objects $([1],1)$ and $([0],0)$ and maps to $a$ and $m$, respectively. No claim that the displayed functors themselves are categorical fibrations is made; the approximation definition allows categorical-fibration replacement.

Their inert markings have the following explicit description. A top edge $([n],1)\to([m],1)$ is marked exactly when $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ is an interval inclusion, that is $\alpha(j)=\alpha(0)+j$ for every $j$. A bottom edge $([n],0)\to([m],0)$ is marked exactly when $\alpha$ is an interval inclusion with $\alpha(m)=n$. Every vertical edge $([n],0)\to([n],1)$ is marked. A cross edge $([n],0)\to([m],1)$ is marked exactly when $\alpha$ is an interval inclusion; it factors as the vertical edge at $[n]$ followed by that marked top edge. All these assertions concern the explicit ordinary operators and their nerves, independently of any target operadic fibration, algebra, module, or section category.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Construction 4.1.2.9 and Proposition 4.1.2.11 (Cut approximation), Construction 4.2.2.6 and Remark 4.2.2.8 (the left-module prism is an approximation); Definition 2.3.3.6 specifies the approximation property. The inert marking is computed from the displayed blocks; compare Remark 4.2.2.26. Online source read; WANTED archive Higher Algebra in literature/. No Stacks tag covers this combinatorial infinity-operadic assertion.

proof.text: First verify the displayed operators, using the ordered-fibre composition of [def-coef-left-module-operadic-encoding]. Identify index $i$ of $\langle n+1\rangle$ with the initial segment $\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\subseteq[n]$, and the basepoint with the empty segment. Inverse image under $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ sends this segment to the segment of length $j$ exactly when $\alpha(j-1)<i\leq\alpha(j)$, to the full segment when $i>\alpha(m)$, and to the empty segment when $i\leq\alpha(0)$. Thus this is precisely LCut, with the full segment the module input. Identifying the empty and full segments gives precisely Cut. Inverse image respects identities and composition, and concatenation of its increasing interval fibres gives the increasing fibre of the composite. The module input is always last in the last nonempty fibre, as required. The quotient identifying the two extreme segments commutes with inverse image; it is exactly $\theta_n$, so $\theta_m\mathrm{LCut}(\beta)=\mathrm{Cut}(\beta)\theta_n$. Consequently the two functors and their natural transformation exist, including $n=0$; their nerves give the stated $\gamma$, since an $r$-simplex in the nerve of a product category is a pair of functors $[r]\to\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $[r]\to[1]$.

source.place: Constructions 4.1.2.9 and 4.2.2.6; Remark 4.2.2.8, inverse-image construction and natural quotient.

proof.text: We will use an explicit ordinary-category form of [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-mapping-criterion]. For any ordinary functor $G:E\to B$, its nerve is an inner fibration: an inner horn contains the composable spine, whose composite arrows uniquely complete it; the triangle relations are composition, and in dimension three the remaining relation is associativity. In higher dimensions every triangle already occurs in the horn. The image of this unique completion is the prescribed base simplex, since a nerve simplex is determined by its spine. Moreover the right-pinched mapping space of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] in $N(E)$ is the constant simplicial set on $\operatorname{Hom}_E(x,y)$: its initial arrows are identities, and all arrows to the final vertex are the same arrow $x\to y$. Apply the cited criterion to these discrete mapping spaces. A homotopy pullback is then an ordinary pullback of sets, since a path in a discrete set is constant. Hence an arrow is $N(G)$-cocartesian exactly when the ordinary post-factorization is unique for every compatible arrow and prescribed base arrow. Apply the same criterion to $G^{\mathrm{op}}$ for the cartesian version: reversing vertices interchanges the initial and final horn conditions of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations]. Explicitly $e:x\to y$ is $N(G)$-cartesian exactly when for every $d:z\to y$ and $h:Gz\to Gx$ with $Gd=Ge\circ h$ there is a unique $v:z\to x$ with $ev=d$ and $Gv=h$. For a local cocartesian assertion apply this reasoning in $E\times_B[1]$ over the specified base edge; its nerve is the degreewise pullback, by the definition of a nerve simplex as a functor.

source.place: Ordinary-nerve specialization of Proposition 5.1.2.1; the inner-fibration and discrete-mapping-space calculations are given explicitly here.

proof.text: For either ordinary operator $H:J\to P$ ($J=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, $P=\mathsf{Assoc}^{\otimes}$ for Cut; $J=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\times[1]$, $P=\mathsf{LM}^{\otimes}$ for the prism), form $J^H$ with objects $(j,w,\sigma)$, where $\sigma:H(j)\xrightarrow{\sim}w$ is a colour-preserving pointed bijection. An arrow to $(j',w',\sigma')$ is $u:j\to j'$ together with $v:w\to w'$ satisfying $v\sigma=\sigma'H(u)$; thus $v$ is determined by $u$. Define $Q:J^H\to P$ by $(j,w,\sigma)\mapsto w$. The inclusion $j\mapsto(j,H(j),1)$ and the forgetful functor are inverse up to the natural isomorphisms $(1,\sigma):(j,H(j),1)\to(j,w,\sigma)$. Their nerves are coherent inverse equivalences: the ordinary natural isomorphism and its inverse give maps $N(J^H)\times\Delta^1\to N(J^H)$, and the inverse equations give their inverse triangles. The functor $Q$ lifts every isomorphism $t:w\to w'$ by $(1,t):(j,w,\sigma)\to(j,w',t\sigma)$. Its nerve is an inner fibration by step 2; an equivalence edge in an ordinary nerve is exactly an isomorphism, since its inverse triangles are the inverse equations. Hence $N(Q)$ is a categorical fibration in the convention of [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction]. This supplies the required replacement, without asserting that $H$ itself lifts permutations.

source.place: Proposition 4.1.2.11, category of isomorphic relabellings; same construction for Remark 4.2.2.8.

proof.text: Compute the inert markings directly from [def-coef-left-module-operadic-encoding]. First reconcile its singleton-fibre description with operadic inertness in [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction]. An ordered-fibre arrow $f$ above an inert pointed map is cocartesian over that pointed map: for a compatible arrow $g$ out of its source and a prescribed pointed factor $h$ with $\overline g=h\overline f$, every input discarded by $f$ is discarded by $g$. For each output of $g$, replace each input in its ordered fibre by its image under $f$. Each non-basepoint fibre of $f$ is a singleton, so this gives the unique ordered fibre of a factor through $f$. The matched singleton has the same colour at both ends: an algebra output cannot receive a module input, and a module output must receive its unique module input. Hence the reconstructed factor satisfies the module-last rule. Step 2, using [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-mapping-criterion], proves cocartesianness of the nerve edge. Conversely an operadically inert edge lies over an inert pointed map by definition. Thus the markings are exactly the singleton-fibre arrows. For a top arrow the non-basepoint fibres have sizes $\alpha(j)-\alpha(j-1)$, $1\leq j\leq m$; they are all singletons exactly when $\alpha(j)=\alpha(0)+j$. For a bottom arrow there is additionally the module fibre of size $n+1-\alpha(m)$, so inertness requires also $\alpha(m)=n$. Each vertical projection has singleton algebra fibres and discards just the module input, hence is inert. The cross arrow has precisely the same algebra fibres as its top arrow and discards the module input. It is therefore inert exactly for interval inclusions, and the naturality equation in step 1 gives its asserted factorization through the vertical projection at $[n]$. For $m=0$ the top and cross conditions are vacuous, while the bottom condition is $\alpha(0)=n$, as the singleton module fibre requires.

source.place: Construction 4.2.2.6, Remark 4.2.2.8 and the inverse-image marking of Remark 4.2.2.26.

proof.text: Over the object $\langle1\rangle$ the Cut domain has just $[1]$. Its only arrow over the identity pointed map is the identity: the inequalities for its single fibre force $\alpha(0)=0$, $\alpha(1)=1$. In the prism there are just $([1],1)$ and $([0],0)$, mapping to $a$ and $m$. Their endomorphisms over the identity are identities by the same calculation. The only possible cross arrow between them is induced by $[1]\to[0]$; its pointed map sends the module input to $*$, so it is not an arrow of this fibre. There is no arrow in the opposite direction in $[1]$. Thus this fibre is discrete with the stated two objects. The target colour fibres are the corresponding discrete singleton and pair: a map over the identity of $\langle1\rangle$ cannot change colour, and singleton fibres have only one order. The replacement of step 3 leaves these colour fibres unchanged, since a pointed colour-preserving bijection on one input is the identity. The asserted colour equivalences follow.

source.place: Colour-fibre computation in the proof of Proposition 4.1.2.11 and its two-colour analogue in Remark 4.2.2.8.

proof.text: Verify condition (i) of [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction] for $N(Q)$. First take the canonical labels. For Cut at $[n]$, the projection selecting input $i$ is the arrow to $[1]$ given by $[1]\to[n]$, $0\mapsto i-1$, $1\mapsto i$. For the prism at $([n],1)$ use the same top arrow to $([1],1)$. At $([n],0)$ each algebra input $i\leq n$ is selected by that cross arrow to $([1],1)$, and the module input is selected by the bottom arrow to $([0],0)$ induced by $[0]\to[n]$, $0\mapsto n$. These are inert by the singleton-fibre calculations in step 4. For a relabelling $\sigma$ select $\sigma^{-1}(i)$ instead. Over each fixed pointed projection $\rho_i$ there is exactly one arrow from the given source into the matching colour object, and no arrow into the other colour object: a singleton algebra fibre requires the two adjacent endpoints, while a singleton module fibre requires the last endpoint. In the pullback over $\rho_i:\langle r\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$, the target fibre is discrete by step 5. Thus every compatible arrow from our source to an object of the target fibre factors uniquely through the selected arrow: the only nonempty case uses its identity target arrow. There are no base arrows from the target endpoint back to the source endpoint. This is exactly the local cocartesian universal property from step 2. When $r=0$ there are no projections to check.

source.place: Definition 2.3.3.6(1), proof of Proposition 4.1.2.11, and Remark 4.2.2.8; local universal property checked explicitly.

proof.text: For active lifts into Cut or the top of the prism, write the target as $(j_n,w_n,\sigma_n)$ and replace the incoming active arrow $b:w\to w_n$ by $b_0=\sigma_n^{-1}b:w\to H(j_n)$. The normalized active arrow $b_0:w\to(\langle n\rangle,\varnothing)$ has no module inputs: any such input would have to go to $*$, forbidden by active. Let its ordered fibres be lists $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ and let $s=\sum_j|B_j|$. Concatenating these lists is a colour-preserving bijection $\tau:(\langle s\rangle,\varnothing)\xrightarrow{\sim}w$, because active means that no input is discarded. Put $\alpha(0)=0$ and $\alpha(j)=\sum_{l=1}^j|B_l|$. The resulting Cut or top arrow $u:[s]\to[n]$ satisfies $H(u)=b_0\tau$: its canonical interval fibres are sent by $\tau$ to the ordered lists $B_j$. Therefore $b\tau=\sigma_nH(u)$, so $(u,b):(j_s,w,\tau)\to(j_n,w_n,\sigma_n)$ is precisely an arrow of $J^H$ above the original $b$. If the target has $n=0$, active forces $s=0$; the same formula is the identity on $[0]$. Empty $B_j$ give repeated values of $\alpha$, which are allowed monotone operators.

source.place: Proposition 4.1.2.11, prefix-sum construction of active lifts; pure-algebra case of Remark 4.2.2.8.

proof.text: Normalize the target label by $b_0=\sigma_n^{-1}b$ as in step 7. For this active arrow into the bottom object $(\langle n+1\rangle,\{n+1\})$, write its ordered output fibres as $B_1,\ldots,B_n,B_{n+1}$. The algebra-output fibres contain only algebra inputs. Its last fibre contains exactly one module input, last in its fibre order. Since no inputs go to $*$, there is exactly one module input in its whole source. Concatenate the algebra-output lists and then the module-output list; this puts that module input last globally and defines a colour-preserving relabelling $\tau:(\langle s+1\rangle,\{s+1\})\xrightarrow{\sim}w$, where the source has $s$ algebra inputs. Set $\alpha(0)=0$ and $\alpha(j)=\sum_{l=1}^j|B_l|$ for $1\leq j\leq n$, summing just the algebra-output fibres. Then $\alpha(n)\leq s$ and the remaining interval $(\alpha(n),s+1]$ is precisely the ordered module-output fibre. The bottom arrow $u:[s]\to[n]$ with this $\alpha$ satisfies $H(u)=b_0\tau$, including its ordered module-output fibre. Thus $b\tau=\sigma_nH(u)$ and $(u,b):(j_s,w,\tau)\to(j_n,w_n,\sigma_n)$ lifts the original active arrow in $J^H$. The module-only source $s=0$ and the module-only target $n=0$ obey the same formulas, including nonempty module fibres with arbitrarily many algebra inputs.

source.place: Remark 4.2.2.8: active lift by the proof of Proposition 4.1.2.11, with its last fibre required to end in the unique module input.

proof.text: For the lifts of steps 7 and 8, normalize an arbitrary factorization problem by its labels. Write $e:(j_s,w_s,\sigma_s)\to(j_n,w_n,\sigma_n)$ over $b$, and $d:(j_r,w_r,\sigma_r)\to(j_n,w_n,\sigma_n)$ over $d_B$, with $bh_B=d_B$. Put $h=\sigma_s^{-1}h_B\sigma_r$. Cancelling $\sigma_n$ in $b\sigma_s=\sigma_nH(e)$ gives $H(e)h=H(d)$. Thus a factor in $J$ with $ev=d$ and $H(v)=h$ gives the factor $(v,h_B)$ in $J^H$, since its defining equation is $h_B\sigma_r=\sigma_sH(v)$. This correspondence is bijective, because the base arrow is prescribed. The canonical opposite operator $\alpha:[n]\to[s]$ of $e$ satisfies $\alpha(0)=0$, and in the top or Cut case also $\alpha(n)=s$, by steps 7 and 8.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Proposition 4.1.2.11, final cartesian-lift calculation; Remark 4.2.2.8, left-module analogue. Agent expansion of the ordered-fibre calculation; no Stacks tag covers this operator-combinatorial assertion. WANTED archive in literature/.

proof.text: For a canonical competitor with opposite operator $\delta:[n]\to[r]$, write $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ for its source and target prism levels. The existence of the competitor forces $\eta\leq\epsilon$; if $\epsilon=0$ both are zero. In the notation of [lem-coef-lm-algebra-fibre-reconstruction] and [lem-coef-lm-module-fibre-reconstruction], the canonical $H(e)$ is $T_\alpha$ for a top or Cut target and $B_\alpha$ for a bottom target. The competitor is respectively $D^\eta_\delta$ (with $\eta=1$ for Cut) or $B_\delta$. Apply the algebra reconstruction lemma in the first case and the module reconstruction lemma in the second to the normalized equation of step 9. Their endpoint hypotheses are exactly those just checked. They give a monotone $\lambda:[s]\to[r]$ with $H(\lambda^{\mathrm{op}},\eta\to\epsilon)=h$ and $\lambda\alpha=\delta$. Hence $v=(\lambda^{\mathrm{op}},\eta\to\epsilon)$, suppressing levels for Cut, is a factor with $ev=d$ and $H(v)=h$.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Proposition 4.1.2.11, final cartesian-lift calculation; Remark 4.2.2.8, left-module analogue. Agent expansion of the ordered-fibre calculation; no Stacks tag covers this operator-combinatorial assertion. WANTED archive in literature/.

proof.text: This canonical factor is unique. Any other factor has a monotone operator $\mu:[s]\to[r]$ with $\mu\alpha=\delta$. Since $\alpha(0)=0$, its initial value is forced: $\mu(0)=\delta(0)$. Equality $H(v)=h$ forces $\mu(j)-\mu(j-1)=|C_j|$ for each algebra-output fibre $C_j$. Summing gives $\mu(j)=\delta(0)+\sum_{l=1}^j|C_l|=\lambda(j)$ for every $j$. This also handles $s=0$: the initial value alone is forced although the pointed map forgets it. There is at most one level arrow $\eta\to\epsilon$, so the arrow $v$ is unique. The bijection in step 9 then proves uniqueness for every labelled factorization problem.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Proposition 4.1.2.11, final cartesian-lift calculation; Remark 4.2.2.8, left-module analogue. Agent expansion of the ordered-fibre calculation; no Stacks tag covers this operator-combinatorial assertion. WANTED archive in literature/.

proof.text: We have proved that for every competitor and prescribed compatible base arrow there is a unique factor through each lift of steps 7 and 8. Apply the ordinary-nerve cartesian criterion established in step 2, the dual of [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-mapping-criterion], to $Q:J^H\to P$. Consequently these lifts are $N(Q)$-cartesian. This checks all competitors, including cross arrows into a top target and module-only bottom words.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Proposition 4.1.2.11, final cartesian-lift calculation; Remark 4.2.2.8, left-module analogue. Agent expansion of the ordered-fibre calculation; no Stacks tag covers this operator-combinatorial assertion. WANTED archive in literature/.

proof.text: The categorical-fibration replacement in step 3 has the inert colour projections of step 6 and the active cartesian lifts of steps 7–12. These are exactly conditions (i) and (ii) in the approximation definition of [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction]. Thus $N(Q)$ is an approximation and its factorization with the categorical equivalence $N(J)\to N(J^H)$ proves that both original functors are approximations. Step 5 proves their colour-fibre equivalences, and step 4 proves every marking and cross-edge factorization claimed. Everything was computed in the ordinary operator categories and their nerves, so no assumption about a target fibration, section, module or algebra was used.
